evals.name: build-from-scratch
evals.prompt: I've got a game jam this weekend and I want to build a little Wolfenstein-ish maze game in TypeScript that runs in the browser. Nothing fancy — a maze you can walk around in first person, textured walls (I don't have any art, so whatever you can generate), mouse look, and a floor and ceiling that aren't just flat grey. Vite is fine for the build. Can you set the project up and get something I can actually walk around in?
evals.expected_output: A working Vite + TypeScript raycaster project: DDA raycasting with perpendicular distance, textured walls, floor/ceiling casting, collision, mouse look, procedural textures. Should build/typecheck.
expectations: Wall distance is perpendicular to the camera plane (DDA sideDist form or an explicit cosine correction), not raw Euclidean distance to the hit point
Pixel writes into a Uint32Array view of ImageData use little-endian (ABGR) byte order or go through a helper that handles endianness; per-byte RGBA writes also count
Floor and ceiling are textured or shaded per row rather than filled with two flat colours
Wall textures are generated in code, so the game runs with no external image files
Player collision resolves the X and Y axes separately so the player slides along walls instead of sticking
The simulation is frame-rate independent (fixed-timestep accumulator or delta-time scaling)
Mouse look is implemented using pointer lock
The project typechecks or builds successfully and the command output is shown

evals.name: debug-broken-raycaster
evals.prompt: Attached is renderer.js from my little maze game and something is off with it. When I stand in a corridor the walls kind of bulge outward at the edges of the screen instead of staying straight, and the enemy sprites show up even when they're behind a wall. Also the whole thing has a weird blue tint that I can't track down — my brick texture is definitely reddish in the source PNG. Can you figure out what's going on and fix it?
evals.expected_output: Identifies fisheye (Euclidean distance / uniform angle sweep instead of perpendicular distance), missing z-buffer test for sprites, and the RGBA byte order bug on little-endian. Provides fixes.
expectations: Diagnoses the bulging walls as fisheye caused by using Euclidean hit distance (and/or a uniform angular sweep) instead of perpendicular distance to the camera plane
Fixes the fisheye by computing perpendicular distance, either the DDA sideDist form or an explicit cosine correction against the view direction
Diagnoses the see-through-wall sprites as a missing per-column depth comparison against wall distances
Adds a z-buffer of per-column wall distances and skips sprite columns whose depth is greater
Diagnoses the blue tint as wrong byte order when writing a Uint32Array view of ImageData on little-endian hardware
Fixes the colour packing to ABGR order, or writes the RGBA bytes individually
The delivered renderer file is valid JavaScript that parses
Explains each root cause rather than only listing the edits

evals.name: grid-locked-dungeon-crawler
evals.prompt: I want to make a slow dark dungeon crawler in TypeScript, the old King's Field / Eye of the Beholder kind of thing where you move square by square rather than sliding around freely. So: step one tile at a time, turn in 90 degree increments, and it should be really dark more than a couple of tiles out so you feel boxed in. I also want doors that need a key to open and a chest or two. Can you build the movement, the lighting and the door/chest interaction?
evals.expected_output: Grid-locked movement with tweened steps and 90-degree snap turns, exponential distance darkness, doors that clear their wall tile and require a key, chests with contents, interaction check for what is in front of the player.
expectations: The player is locked to tile centres with a discrete facing rather than moving continuously
A step is an animated one-tile transition over time, not an instant teleport
Turning is in 90-degree increments and the camera angle interpolates smoothly through the turn
New movement input is refused while a step or turn is still in progress
Distance darkness uses an exponential or similarly steep falloff so geometry a few tiles out is near-black
Opening a door modifies the wall grid, so rendering, collision and line of sight all update from one change
A locked door requires a matching key from the player's inventory
There is an explicit check of what occupies the cell in front of the player, driving an interaction prompt
A chest yields its contents only once
The project typechecks or builds successfully and the command output is shown
